idiom_name: weak.Pointer[T] via weak.Make / Value (Go 1.24+) plus runtime.AddCleanup
implementation_notes: Go acquired weak pointers in 1.24: weak.Make(ptr) returns a weak.Pointer[T] whose Value() gives back the original pointer while the object is reachable and nil once it is not, and weak pointers compare by the identity of the object and offset they were made from, so they can be used as map keys - the documented uses are caches, canonicalization maps and tying lifetimes of separate values together. The guarantees are stated plainly in the package docs: Value may return nil as soon as the object becomes unreachable, and it is not guaranteed to ever return nil (tiny pointer-free objects can be batched into an allocation slot that stays alive), so always re-check the promoted pointer and hold it in a local for the duration of the use, with runtime.KeepAlive where the object must remain live until a specific point. runtime.AddCleanup supplies the best-effort notification used to delete a stale cache entry; before Go 1.24 the runtime had no weak pointers at all and unsafe tricks are not a substitute.
pitfalls: Value() may keep returning the object long after the last real reference is gone (nil is not guaranteed, and tiny objects can share an allocation slot), so a cache must be able to evict without waiting for nil.
Keep the promoted pointer in a local and call runtime.KeepAlive after the last point where the object must stay reachable, otherwise it can be collected while the function still runs.
weak.Make forces the value to escape to the heap, and the pointer identifies an object plus offset - weak pointers to different fields of one struct do not compare equal.
